claim: A flat decal card placed on a compound-curved surface visibly floats/clips at its corners because it's still planar geometry. DECALmachine's 'Project' function (pie menu, D) re-subdivides and deforms the decal's own geometry to shrinkwrap it directly onto the underlying surface's curvature, restoring seamless contact instead of leaving a rigid flat card resting on top.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation (2026-08-14, watched full video): at 4:00-4:30, a decal's corners visibly float above a curved shoulder plate before Project is applied; after Project, the decal's geometry subdivides and deforms to match the surface, eliminating the floating/clipping.
rejected_alternative: Leaving a flat decal card resting on a curved surface without projecting it
reason: A rigid planar decal can't follow curvature and will float or clip at its edges; projecting deforms the decal's own mesh to match the target surface.

claim: For a reusable 3D kitbash hardware piece (bolt, greeble) intended to snap onto varied curved surfaces: set the object's origin to its flat contact face, then in a vertex group assign descending weights outward-to-inward across concentric rings of the base flange (e.g. 1.0 at the outer perimeter ring, stepping down to 0.2 near the center) -- when later deformed to match a target surface, only the outer skirt (high weight) blends into the hull while the rigid functional core (low/zero weight) stays undistorted.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 5:32-7:05, a vertex group is assigned stepped weights (1.0 down to 0.2) across concentric loop rings from the outer flange inward to the central bolt, specifically to control how much of the piece deforms when later snapped to a curved hull.
rejected_alternative: Applying uniform full-strength deformation across the entire kitbash piece
reason: A uniformly-weighted deformation would warp the piece's functional core along with its contact flange; graduated weights isolate the deformation to just the outer skirt that actually needs to conform.

claim: To attach a separately-modeled 3D hardware piece (bolt, vent, bracket) seamlessly onto a curved hull without booleans or retopology: add a Shrinkwrap modifier restricted to the piece's weighted contact vertex group targeting the hull, then add a Data Transfer modifier below it (Source = hull, same vertex group, Face Corner Data > Custom Normals > Nearest Face Interpolated) -- the Shrinkwrap handles position, the Data Transfer handles matching normals, and together they eliminate the harsh dark shading seam that Shrinkwrap alone leaves at the contact boundary.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 7:15-8:50, Shrinkwrap alone snaps a bolt's contact rim to a hull but leaves a harsh dark shading seam; adding Data Transfer with interpolated custom normals from the hull, restricted to the same vertex group, matches the specular highlight across the boundary seamlessly.
rejected_alternative: Using Shrinkwrap alone to attach the piece to the hull
reason: Shrinkwrap matches vertex position but not surface normals, leaving a visible shading break; Data Transfer specifically fixes the normal mismatch that Shrinkwrap doesn't address. This is now the third independent source converging on this exact Shrinkwrap+Data-Transfer-custom-normals combination for seamless floating-detail attachment. CORRECTION (2026-08-14, live user demonstration, see runs/2026-08-14_shrinkwrap-vs-join-handle-correction/): 'seamless' here means seamless SHADING between two still-separate objects, not one merged mesh. Attempted as a fix for the mug build's handle-attachment problem and directly corrected: a part that needs to read as structurally fused (a handle) requires join+bridge into genuine single-mesh connected topology, which this technique does not produce no matter how well the contact points and normals conform. Valid scope stays genuinely separate detail parts (bolts, vents, brackets, decals) -- the same use cases all three converging sources actually demonstrate.

claim: For a non-destructive, easily-redesignable panel seam/shutline on a curved body (e.g. a car door gap): build the seam as a single open 1D edge path (not by cutting loops into the body's own topology), add a Screw modifier with Angle 0 and a small Screw depth (pure vertical extrusion, no rotation) to give it height, add a Solidify modifier to set the gap's wall thickness, then boolean-difference this cutter against the body -- the seam's shape and width can be redesigned at any time just by moving the original edge path's vertices, since the actual cutting geometry is generated procedurally.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 16:05-17:35, a flat 1D edge path drives a Screw modifier (angle 0, small depth) plus Solidify to generate a boolean cutter for a car panel seam, letting the seam be reshaped later by moving a couple of vertices instead of manually re-cutting topology.
rejected_alternative: Manually cutting topology loops directly into the curved body to create the panel seam
reason: Manually cut loops into a curved surface disrupt edge flow and risk pinching under subdivision/smooth shading; a procedurally-generated cutter derived from a simple edge path avoids touching the body's own topology at all and stays fully editable.

claim: When a boolean panel-seam cutter (built via Screw + Solidify from a 1D path) has sharp, artificial 90-degree interior corners, add a Bevel modifier to the CUTTER mesh and place it ABOVE Solidify in the stack (order: Bevel, then Solidify, then Boolean) -- beveling the 2D path's vertices before wall thickness is generated produces smoothly radiused interior corners in the final cut, rather than beveling after solidification which would not round the corners the same way.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 18:25-18:50, a Bevel modifier is added to the panel-cutter mesh above Solidify in the stack, and increasing its segment count visibly rounds the sharp interior corners of the resulting boolean cut in real time.
rejected_alternative: Beveling the cutter after Solidify, or not beveling the cutter's corners at all
reason: Modifier stack order changes what geometry the bevel actually rounds -- beveling before Solidify rounds the original path's corner vertices, producing clean radiused corners in the final solidified/booleaned cut.

claim: To build a braided/diamond-lattice conduit sleeve that follows a curved cable path: take a capped cylinder, remove its end caps, run Poke Faces (adds a center vertex per face, creating triangle fans) then Triangulate to Quads (converts the resulting triangles into a diagonal diamond pattern), then Wireframe (converts the diamond edges into an actual lattice-cage mesh) -- then attach this sleeve mesh to a curve (e.g. via the Cablerator add-on's 'Add as Edit Segment') so it arrays and deforms automatically along the cable's path, with an adjustable offset to slide it along the hose.
supporting_evidence: Gemini video-understanding observation: at 27:10-28:50, a 16-sided uncapped cylinder is run through Poke Faces > Triangulate to Quads > Wireframe to produce a diamond-lattice mesh, then attached to a Cablerator curve segment so it deforms along the cable's trajectory.
rejected_alternative: Manually modeling a braided sleeve pattern by hand along a curved path
reason: Manually building a diamond-braid pattern that correctly deforms along an arbitrary 3D curve is tedious; the Poke > Tri-to-Quads > Wireframe sequence generates the lattice pattern procedurally, and curve-segment tools handle the deformation automatically.
